readings.title: A box of stories from the neighborhood
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When the old Riverside cinema was scheduled for renovation, historian Marta asked residents to share memories of the building. She expected stories about famous films. Instead, many people described their first paid job at the ticket desk, a rainy afternoon with a grandparent, or the friend they met in the queue. These accounts suggested that a public building could matter for reasons absent from its architectural record.

Marta invited contributors to a recording session at the library. Before each conversation, she explained how the recording might be used and asked whether the speaker wanted a real name attached. Some people agreed to public access, while others allowed only written extracts. A few decided not to participate after hearing the options. Their decision was respected, and no recording was kept without an agreement. The project aimed to preserve memories, not to make private experiences public by default.

The stories also raised questions about accuracy. Two speakers remembered the same concert in different years. Rather than silently choosing one account, Marta checked newspaper notices and added a note explaining the difference. She did not remove the personal memories, because they still showed what the event had meant to the speakers. The archive distinguished a documented date from a remembered impression, allowing readers to understand both.

At the renovation exhibition, visitors could listen to selected recordings beside photographs of the building. Short written summaries were provided for those who could not hear the audio easily. Marta hoped the collection would continue after the exhibition closed. Its purpose was not to create one perfect story of the cinema. It was to preserve a range of experiences, with clear information about where they came from and how people had agreed to share them.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: Checking comfort in a public building
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A public service center received repeated complaints that its waiting room was too warm in winter. The building manager, Owen, considered lowering the heating throughout the building. Before doing so, he asked staff to record temperatures in different rooms at regular times. They also noted whether windows were open and how many people were present. The aim was to understand where and when discomfort occurred, rather than assume that every room had the same problem.

The records showed a clear pattern. The waiting room became warm around midday when sunlight entered its large windows and visitor numbers increased. Meanwhile, a small office on the north side remained cool. Reducing the whole building's heating would have made that office uncomfortable without fully addressing the waiting room. Owen adjusted the local controls and arranged for a faulty window blind to be repaired.

After the changes, staff repeated the observations for several weeks. They asked visitors a short question about comfort as well as recording temperature. Owen explained that a number on a thermometer could not capture every experience. Someone who had walked quickly from a bus stop might feel warmer than a person who had been sitting still for half an hour. Comments helped interpret the measurements, though no single comment was treated as a complete description of conditions.

Energy use fell slightly, but Owen was cautious about claiming the adjustments caused the entire reduction. The second period had also been warmer outdoors. A fair comparison needed to account for weather and opening hours. The exercise still had practical value: fewer visitors complained, and the north office remained comfortable. It showed that a focused change, informed by several kinds of evidence, could work better than one large adjustment applied everywhere.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

readings.title: The shelf that welcomed experiments
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
In a small bookshop, owner Saira noticed that customers often bought familiar authors and ignored unfamiliar titles. She understood the hesitation: readers had limited time and did not want to spend money on a disappointing choice. To encourage exploration, she placed a shelf near the entrance with short, handwritten recommendations. Each card described the reading experience rather than claiming that the book was the best of its kind.

One card said a novel moved slowly but offered memorable conversations. Another described a history book as demanding at first, with clear maps that rewarded patient reading. Saira included reservations because she wanted customers to judge whether a book suited them. A glowing recommendation without any detail might attract attention, but it did little to explain what a reader would actually encounter. Staff signed their cards so regular visitors could learn whose tastes they shared.

The shop also invited customers to write recommendations after finishing a book. Saira asked them to avoid revealing major plot developments and to state what they enjoyed or found difficult. Some cards disagreed strongly about the same title. She displayed contrasting views together instead of selecting only praise. The disagreement often led to useful conversations at the counter and reminded customers that a book's value could depend on a reader's interests and expectations.

Sales from the shelf grew gradually, but Saira did not treat sales as its only purpose. Some visitors borrowed a recommended title from the library and later returned to discuss it. The shelf helped the shop become a place where people could talk honestly about reading. It did not remove the risk of disappointment. It made the decision more informed and gave unfamiliar books a chance to reach readers who might otherwise have walked past them.

readings.title: Rain measurements behind the school
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A science teacher named Joel placed a simple rain gauge behind the school and invited his class to record daily rainfall. The activity seemed straightforward: look at the scale, write down a number, and empty the container. During the first week, however, the class recorded an unusually large amount on a dry morning. A student then admitted that the container had not been emptied the previous day. The number represented two days of rain, not one.

Instead of treating the mistake only as carelessness, Joel used it to discuss measurement. The class agreed on a fixed reading time and a rotating pair of observers. One student read the scale while the other checked the entry and emptied the gauge. They marked weekends as unobserved unless someone had specifically arranged to attend. A missing daily measurement was not recorded as zero, because absence of observation did not establish absence of rain.

Placement mattered as well. The first location was close to a tree, whose branches could block some rain or release extra drops after a shower. The class moved the gauge to a more open area and wrote down the date of the change. Joel warned them that readings before and after the move might not be directly comparable. Keeping a note of the method was as important as keeping the numbers themselves.

By the end of term, the students had a chart with gaps, corrections, and a clear record of how observations were made. It looked less tidy than a perfectly filled table. Yet Joel considered it a stronger piece of work because its limits were visible. The class had learned that useful evidence depends on consistent methods and honest records, and that understanding a mistake can improve the next measurement.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节与推断

translation.stem: Personal memories help us understand how people experienced the past, but they do not always provide exact dates or complete explanations. Two people may remember the same event differently because they noticed different details or gave those details different meanings. This does not make their stories worthless. It means that listeners should ask careful questions and compare memories with other records when possible. Respect is equally important. Before sharing an interview publicly, an organizer should explain who may hear it and how it will be used. A collection becomes more trustworthy when its sources and limits are clear. Preserving history involves both protecting useful information and respecting the people whose experiences give that information its human meaning.
translation.referenceAnswer: 个人记忆帮助我们理解人们如何经历过去，却不总能提供准确日期或完整解释。两个人对同一事件的记忆可能不同，因为他们注意到了不同细节，或赋予细节不同意义。这并不意味着故事毫无价值，而是说听者应认真提问，并在可能时将记忆与其他记录比较。尊重同样重要。公开分享访谈前，组织者应说明谁可能听到以及如何使用。资料来源和局限清楚时，收藏就更加可信。保存历史既要保护有用信息，也要尊重那些以自身经历赋予信息人文意义的人。
translation.explanation: 注意 worthless 的否定范围，both...and 的并列，以及 whose 引导的定语从句。

writing.stem: Write an essay entitled Learning from a Small Mistake. Describe a mistake in study or everyday work, explain what it taught you, and suggest a way to prevent a similar problem. Write at least 100 English words.
writing.sampleAnswer:
Last month I sent my study group a timetable with the wrong meeting room. I had copied an older message without checking the latest booking. Two classmates went to the wrong building and missed the beginning of our discussion. Although the mistake was small, it wasted their time and made our work less organized.

I apologized and sent the corrected information as soon as I noticed the problem. The experience taught me that familiar details still need attention. Now I check the room, date, and time against the current booking before sending an invitation. I also ask one classmate to read important arrangements. A mistake cannot always be undone, but an honest response and a simple change in routine can make it useful for future learning.
writing.explanation: 具体描述错误、影响与补救，重点写从中形成的可执行习惯。
